rashi:a1.1: Ten years Samuel reigned by himself: alone, without Saul; therefore the tenth year is not counted within those forty years. Thirty-seven David reigned: before Absalom’s rebellion. My teacher explained this matter elsewhere thus: the tenth year of Samuel was [the tenth] of Samuel’s greatness. We do not derive it explicitly from a verse, only because one cannot find forty years by any other count. Go and calculate from the death of Eli, which is the start of Samuel’s greatness, until the year of Absalom’s rebellion: forty-nine years, thirteen for Samuel and Saul and thirty-six for David. Eli died when the Ark was captured, as it is stated: “And it came to pass, when he made mention [of the Ark of God, that he fell]” (I Samuel 4:18); and it is written: “And the Ark of the Lord was in the field of the Philistines seven months” (I Samuel 6:1); the Philistines brought it back, “and the men of Kiriath-jearim came” (I Samuel 7:1). When David reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel he brought the Ark from there, as it is written: “And David again [gathered]” (II Samuel 6:1); and it is written: “And it came to pass, from the day that the Ark abode in Kiriath-jearim, that the time was long, for it was twenty years” (I Samuel 7:2). Subtract from them the seven years that David reigned in Hebron. Of the rest, Samuel reigned by himself eleven years, and Saul with Samuel two years, as it is written: “And two years he reigned” (I Samuel 13:1). Samuel died only four months before Saul, for so it is explicit in the book of Samuel: “And Samuel died” (I Samuel 25:1), and after it is written: “And David said: I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul” (I Samuel 27:1), and he fled to Achish until Saul died; and it is written: “And the number of the days that David dwelt in the field of the Philistines was a full year and four months” (I Samuel 27:7). We have found thirteen years for Samuel and Saul from the death of Eli until David reigned, and thirty-six for David when Absalom rebelled: that is forty[-nine], etc. Subtract the nine years of Samuel before they asked for a king: that leaves forty years from when they asked for the kingship until the year of Absalom’s rebellion, inclusive. And so it is taught in Seder Olam: it was the thirty-sixth year of David’s reign. And this is the reading: “Ten years Samuel reigned by himself, and one year that Saul reigned by himself, and thirty-six for David.” I have added to this on my own: go and calculate also from the birth of Samuel, and you will likewise find that Samuel held authority over Israel thirteen years. For the Master said in Seder Olam: “Now Eli the priest sat upon the seat … and she was in bitterness of soul” (I Samuel 1:9–10), and in that year Eli was appointed judge over Israel, and he judged Israel forty years. Subtract one year for [Samuel’s] gestation: Samuel was thus thirty-nine when he prophesied and rose to greatness, for when Eli died, Samuel’s sun shone, thirteen years of his authority. For all his years were only fifty-two, as we derive elsewhere (Mo’ed Katan) from “until the child is weaned” (I Samuel 1:22), that is twenty-four months, the nursing period of a child, and then “and there abide forever,” the “forever” of a Jubilee, that is fifty years. Within these thirteen years were included the two years that Saul reigned, for both died in one year, as explained above.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Tosafot’s reading is “thirty-six that David reigned,” and that makes forty years from when they asked for a king, with Samuel’s tenth year, in which they asked, counted among the forty. How do we know Samuel judged Israel thirteen years? Eli died when the Ark was captured, and Samuel was appointed immediately after; the Ark was in the field of the Philistines seven months and then in Kiriath-jearim, from where David took it to Jerusalem once he reigned over all Israel (II Samuel 6:1), and it was there twenty years (I Samuel 7:2). Subtract David’s seven years in Hebron: thirteen years remain for Samuel and Saul, from Eli’s death until Saul died and David reigned in Hebron. Of them Samuel reigned by himself ten years; one year Samuel and Saul reigned (the year Samuel anointed him was not a full year for Saul, since for part of it Samuel led Israel); and two years Saul reigned by himself, while Samuel was still alive, for Samuel died only four months before Saul (I Samuel 25:1; 27:1; 27:7). Thirteen for Samuel and Saul and thirty-six for David until Absalom rebelled make forty-nine; subtract the nine years before they asked for a king, since they asked in the tenth year and the tenth counts, and forty remain until the rebellion, inclusive. Difficulty on this: Seder Olam teaches that David reigned five years after the rebellion: three years of famine (II Samuel 21:1), a year of the census, “at the end of nine months” (II Samuel 24:8), and a year in which he set up the priestly watches, “in the fortieth year of the reign of David” (I Chronicles 26:31). One must say that the year of the rebellion was the first year of the famine. Some books read “thirty-seven that David reigned”; on that reading one must say the famine began one year before the rebellion, and that Samuel’s tenth year, when they asked for a king, is not counted among the forty: one counts only three years of Saul and thirty-seven of David, making forty. In Seder Olam Rabbi Nehorai says the rebellion was in the thirty-fifth year of David’s reign; on his view we do not find forty years from the request for a king to the rebellion. Some explain the thirteen years of Samuel from his lifespan: all the years of Samuel of Ramah were fifty-two, since when he was weaned Hannah brought him [to Eli], presumably at two, the usual nursing period, and it is written “and there abide forever” (I Samuel 1:22), fifty years, the “forever” of a Jubilee. Hannah’s prayer was on the day Eli was appointed, and Eli judged Israel forty years; subtract a year for Samuel’s gestation, and thirty-nine remain of Eli’s, leaving thirteen for Samuel, who was appointed as soon as Eli died, as the Master said (Kiddushin 72b): “The sun also rises and the sun goes down” – before Eli’s sun set, Samuel’s sun rose. So Samuel’s authority began when he was thirty-nine and lasted thirteen years. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: Thirty-seven that David reigned: and at that time Absalom said to his father, “Let me go, I pray you” [and pay my vow] (II Samuel 15:7).
rashi:a2.1: Whose owner achieved atonement: it was lost, he achieved atonement with another, and the first was found.
rashi:a2.2: And a communal one: where they achieved atonement with another.
rashi:a2.3: Does not die: for [the rule of] the sin offerings that die is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai [the printed text adds in parentheses: “the inner ones”], in this tractate, and the first tanna holds that it was learned of an individual and not of a community.
rashi:a3.1: Shall die: for it was learned of a community too.
rashi:a3.2: Rabbi Shimon says: Just as we found, etc.: that is to say, we hold that five sin offerings die: a sin offering whose owner died, one whose owner achieved atonement, one whose year has passed, the offspring of a sin offering and the substitute for a sin offering. Three of them were not learned of a community, because they cannot be found among communal offerings: the offspring of a sin offering cannot be found in a community, since there is no female among communal offerings; the substitute for a sin offering neither, since a communal offering does not render a substitute; and one whose owner died, since the community does not die, as we say below in the Gemara.
rashi:a3.3: So too one whose owner achieved atonement and one whose year has passed: even though we can find them in a community, it was not learned that they die.
rashi:a4.1: What does it say: “sin offering … he shall bring”: why do I need it to write “And if he bring a lamb as his offering for a sin offering” (Leviticus 4:32)? Let it write: “And if a lamb be his offering for a sin offering,” and so on.
rashi:a4.2: He shall bring it: the end of the verse: “a female without blemish he shall bring it.”
rashi:a5.1: Rabbi Shimon says: It shall die: for it is an individual sin offering whose owner achieved atonement.
rashi:a6.1: But didn’t Rabbi Yehuda say “shall die”: for so you heard from him in the mishna, even of a community, and all the more so of an individual.
rashi:a6.2: But didn’t Rabbi Shimon say: in the mishna, of an individual: five sin offerings die. He counts this sin offering whose owner achieved atonement, and teaches “the matters are stated of an individual.”
rashi:a7.1: Lost at the time of separation: and not at the time of atonement, since the first was found before he achieved atonement with the second, as the baraita teaches. In that case Rabbi Yehuda says it grazes, for according to Rabbi Yehuda it was learned that it dies only where it was found after the owner achieved atonement. And where the mishna teaches “shall die,” it is speaking of one lost at the time of atonement. That is our reading: even at the time he achieved atonement with the second, the first was still lost.
rashi:a8.1: Both this and that at the time of separation: it was found before the second was used for atonement. The mishna, which says “shall die” according to Rabbi Yehuda: Rabbi Yehuda says it according to Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], who says below in the chapter Velad Ḥatat (Temurah 22b), in the mishna, that one lost at the time of separation dies even though it was found before atonement. The baraita, where Rabbi Yehuda says it grazes: he says it according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi, who say a sin offering dies only if it was found after the owner achieved atonement.
rashi:a9.1: But is there one who says, etc.: he raises the difficulty against the mishna.
gershom:a2.1: Rabbi Shimon says: Just as we found with the offspring of a sin offering, the substitute for a sin offering and a sin offering whose owner died, which die, that the matters are stated of an individual and not of a community. So Rabbi Shimon explains in the Gemara, in a baraita. And you cannot speak of the offspring of a sin offering in a community, since a communal sin offering is not a female, etc.
gershom:a3.1: So too a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement and one whose year has passed, which die: the matters are stated of an individual and not of a community. What does it say: “sin offering … he shall bring”: that is to say, why is it needed to write “And if he bring a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, a female without blemish he shall bring it”? Let it write: “And if a lamb be his offering for a sin offering, a female without blemish he shall bring it.” [A note in the printed text says a heading is missing here and supplies: “But Rabbi Yehuda, we heard from him ‘shall die’ even of a communal sin offering, and all the more so a sin offering, etc.”] All the more so an individual’s sin offering whose owner achieved atonement dies, since about an individual they do not disagree.
gershom:a4.1: And it is not difficult: where Rabbi Yehuda says it grazes, here it is speaking of one lost and found at the time the second was separated, before it was sacrificed. Since he may sacrifice whichever he wishes, the second does not die but grazes.
gershom:a5.1: Here it is speaking of one lost and found not at the time of separation but after the sacrifice, when he had already achieved atonement; therefore it dies.
gershom:a6.1: And if you wish, say: both this and that: where it was found at the time of separation.
gershom:a7.1: And it is not difficult: where it teaches “grazes,” that is Rabbi Yehuda according to the Rabbis, as we learned in the chapter Velad Ḥatat: One who separates a sin offering and it was lost, and he separated another in its place, and he did not manage to sacrifice it before the first was found, and both are unblemished: one of them is sacrificed as a sin offering and the second dies; this is the statement of Rabbi. And the Rabbis say: A sin offering dies only if it was found, etc. And where it teaches “dies,” that is Rabbi Yehuda according to Rabbi.
rashi:b1.1: Similarly: it is not explained what this refers to.
tosafot:b1.1: Similarly, Rabbi Yosei said: Rashi explains that it is not explained what this refers to. But so it is taught in Torat Kohanim, on the one who expounds the verse written about [the sliding-scale offering]: “And the second he shall make a burnt offering” (Leviticus 5:10): just as a burnt offering is not eaten, so too this sin offering is not eaten. It is taught there, on that.
rashi:b2.1: But is a sin offering sacrificed as a burnt offering: for it is written: “twelve goats for a sin offering; all a burnt offering.”
rashi:b2.2: So too that sin offering is not eaten, as Rabbi Yosei would say: they brought the goats for idol worship, corresponding to the twelve tribes, who had worshipped idols in the days of Zedekiah. A community brings a goat as a sin offering, as it is written about idol worship in the portion of Shelaḥ Lekha: “all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering … and one he-goat for a sin offering” (Numbers 15:24). Those goats are burned outside the camp like the bull for an unwitting communal sin, and they are the “goats that are burned,” as we say in the chapter Eizehu Mekoman (Zevachim 47a). In Menachot, in the chapter HaKometz Rabba (Menachot 27a), we derive it from the verse written about the bull for an unwitting communal sin: “Thus shall he do with the bull; as he did [with the bull of the sin offering]” (Leviticus 4:20). So it is taught: “As he did”: what does the verse teach? To repeat the sprinklings, etc.; and the end of that baraita: “the sin offering” – to include the goats of idol worship, to be treated like the bull for an unwitting communal sin.
tosafot:b2.1: For idol worship they committed in the days of Zedekiah: this follows the one who holds that for a community’s idol worship each and every tribe brings a bull and a goat; for that reason they brought twelve goats as sin offerings, for the twelve tribes.
gershom:b1.1: So too the sin offering is not eaten, since they brought them for idol worship: and they were goats that are burned.
rashi:b3.1: And yet they were sacrificed: even though the owners had died during those seventy years they were in Babylonia.
tosafot:b3.1: It might enter our mind that the one who holds a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement dies also holds a sin offering whose owners died dies: And if you say: then let it be difficult for the mishna too, for on this no one disagrees, that of a sin offering whose owner died the matter is stated of an individual and not of a community, and even so they disagree about one whose owners achieved atonement! One can say it is not comparable. The mishna takes it as obvious that a sin offering whose owners died does not exist in a community, meaning where all the owners died and not one of them remained. But here it entered our mind [that it is a case where] some of the owners are still alive, and that is why it says “and yet they were sacrificed.”
tosafot:b3.2: But here there is a case whose owners died, and yet it was sacrificed: The Rashba asked: what does this have to do with “owners died”? Throughout the Talmud it speaks of one who separated a sin offering and afterward its owners died, but here they had separated nothing! And Rabbeinu Netanel says: if one may sacrifice even without having separated, evidently there is atonement for the dead; and if so, all the more so where he separated and afterward its owners died, it is fit to be sacrificed. So it is implied in the first chapter of Horayot (6a), which says “But there is atonement for the dead” and cites this passage from here: this implies that if there is atonement for the dead, it is the sons’ duty to sacrifice for them, and all the more so if he separated and afterward died, it is the sons’ duty to sacrifice them.
tosafot:b3.3: And yet it was sacrificed: And if you say: let it be difficult also for the one who says it grazes, for no one says it may be sacrificed! One can say: certainly, since it does not go to its death, it is fit even to be sacrificed. So we find in the chapter Hotzi’u Lo (Yoma 50a), about the statement concerning the bull, “and even with its blood”: the Gemara objects, but it is a sin offering whose owner died! And it answers: since it also comes for the atonement of the community, it is not one whose owner died. Evidently, where it does not go to its death, it is fit even to be sacrificed.
gershom:b2.1: But here the owners died: the generation of Zedekiah, and yet it was sacrificed; this is difficult for Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:b3.1: Rav Pappa said: even [according to the one who says a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement dies], etc.: and there is nothing to infer from this case, since there is no rule of dying in a community; and it is not difficult for Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:b4.1: If we say because it is written: “Instead of your fathers shall be your sons”: for the son is in his father’s place, and it is not as if he were dead.
gershom:b5.1: If so, even an individual as well: let us say that a son stands in his father’s place, and it should not count as a sin offering whose owner died.
rashi:b5.1: Your sons shall be: that is to say, the sons are in their place, and for that reason their sin offering is sacrificed.
rashi:b6.1: This is the reason that the community does not die: that there is no rule of a sin offering whose owner died in a community. It is derived from the additional-offering goats of the Festivals and New Moons, which are sin offerings, and the Merciful One said: bring them from the collection of the chamber, from the shekels that come in Adar. Yet one could say: perhaps the owners of those coins died – some of those who brought the shekels died before the Festivals, and it turns out that they are sacrificing a sin offering whose owners died, since they have a share in it.
gershom:b6.1: For the Merciful One said to bring it from the collection of the chamber, as it is written: “This is the burnt offering of every New Moon in its month” (Numbers 28:14): renew [the funds] and bring an offering from the new collection.
gershom:b7.1: And perhaps the owners of these coins died: rather, conclude from it that there is no rule of death in a community.
rashi:b7.1: When they sacrificed: these goats for idol worship, in the days of Ezra.
rashi:b7.2: They sacrificed them for the living: on behalf of those still alive of those who worshipped idols in the days of Zedekiah.
rashi:b7.3: And many shouted: those who had not seen the First Temple were now shouting and rejoicing.
gershom:b8.1: And if you wish, say: when they sacrificed these sin offerings, the goats for idol worship, they sacrificed them for the living who remained from that generation, so it was not a sin offering whose owners died. And as for what you derive from the New Moon goat: perhaps the New Moon goat is different, since the majority of the community who consecrated those coins is alive; and in the days of Ezra too, the majority of the community of Zedekiah’s generation was still alive. And how could they sacrifice an offering for idol worship, when they were intentional?
rashi:b8.1: But perhaps those: who were still alive were a minority of Israel, and a minority does not bring offerings as a majority does but as individuals, each one a female goat. Since they brought goats, a goat for each tribe, as a majority does, they certainly relied on the earlier ones who had died; and conclude from it that a communal sin offering does not die.
rashi:b8.2: From the noise of the weeping of the people: evidently those weeping were many compared with those shouting, and those weeping were of the earlier ones.
rashi:b9.1: But they were intentional: in the days of Zedekiah.
gershom:b9.1: It was a provisional edict: beyond the letter of the law.
rashi:b10.1: This also stands to reason: that it was a provisional edict.
rashi:b10.2: Granted, twelve bulls: for a burnt offering, and twelve goats for a sin offering.
rashi:b10.3: Corresponding to the twelve tribes: for this is the communal offering for idol worship, a bull for a burnt offering and a goat for a sin offering, in the portion of Shelaḥ Lekha.
rashi:b11.1: Who contains all: Torah, fear of sin and acts of kindness.
gershom:b10.1: Would study Torah: precisely, like Moses.
rashi:b13.1: Those that were forgotten, were forgotten: the ones they forgot.
rashi:b13.2: And those that they studied: the ones they did not forget, they studied like Moses.
gershom:b11.1: If the majority deem it pure, [they purified it]: evidently it was not as clear to them as it was to Moses.
rashi:b15.1: The heart was diminished: the heart had grown less, and they did not know how to restore those they had forgotten through the dialectic of the halakha, how it went; so they were divided over them and followed the majority.
rashi:b15.2: They would study: those that were not forgotten, they studied like Moses.
tosafot:b15.1: The heart was diminished: they did not have the heart to restore what they had forgotten, and on this they were divided.
tosafot:b15.2: They would study: what remained to them that they had not forgotten, they studied with precision, like Moses.
gershom:b12.1: What was forgotten: in the days of his mourning; of that it says: if the majority deem it pure, they purified it. Another version: this applies where the heart was diminished – that too refers to the halakhot forgotten in the days of mourning for Moses.
rashi:b16.1: Flaw: it now enters our mind [that this means] there was no flaw of sin in the clusters who stood as leaders of Israel.
rashi:b17.1: Groaning: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) crying out from the pain of his heart, as in “groaning, she groaned,” said of Sisera’s mother (the Targum on Judges 5).
rashi:b18.1: An armed bandit: small livestock cannot be guarded; it goes and grazes in other people’s fields.
rashi:b20.1: And the Sages: these Sages, Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava.
rashi:b20.2: Lived many generations after Yosef ben Yo’ezer: that is to say, these lived many generations after Yosef ben Yo’ezer, and it teaches that they found no sin in them; evidently there was no flaw in them.
gershom:b13.1: And the Sages, Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai or Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, lived generations after Yosef [printed: Yosei] ben Yo’ezer, and no flaw at all was found in them.
